newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE warns against Albania security vacuum.
newsitem.headline: OSCE warns against Albania security vacuum.

text.p: European envoy to Albania Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday the planned withdrawal of international peacekeepers by mid-August risked creating a security vacuum in the troubled Balkan state.
Vranitzky, speaking after a meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's (OSCE) permanent council, warned against leaving Albania in the lurch.
"I firmly believe that it would be a mistake to leave a complete security vacuum," he told reporters.

A United Nations mandate for the Italian-led multi-national protection force runs out on August 12 but the first troops have already begun withdrawing, having ensured the smooth running of recent parliamentary elections.
The collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes earlier this year had plunged Europe's poorest nation into months of rioting and bloodshed.
"I am not suggesting replacing the protection force man for man...but we have to give a lot of thought to what should be done after the troops' withdrawal," Vranitzky said.
He suggested NATO could pick up the slack within the framework of its Partnership for Peace and said his idea had met with a positive response from NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.

"I have proposed that within the Partnership for Peace programme Albania's armed forces could be restructured and restored," Vranitzky said, noting the European Union's defence arm, the WEU, had already made a commitment to train the police.
"Of all the institutions, the police and army deserve special mention. They will have the primary responsibility of tackling security problems in Albania," the former Austrian chancellor said.
An estimated one million guns are in private hands in Albania following an orgy of looting during the unrest.
Vranitzky was to chair a working group later on Thursday that would consider practical ways of aiding Albania's recovery from anarchy.
Representatives from NATO and the WEU were due to attend along with delegates from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the EU and the Council of Europe.

The working group will pave the way for a high-level international conference on Albania in late July. That meeting will assess the post-election situation and discuss further economic and financial aid.
"Albania needs the help of the World Bank, the EU and bilateral help. Albania also needs the Council of Europe, NATO's Partnership for Peace and the WEU," Vranitzky said.
However, he sounded a warning to the nation's fractious politicians.

"I want to state clearly that the winners and losers of the election have to stand up to their democratic responsibilities. Should this not happen, should they return to their old games, the international community will not be willing to cooperate."

The ex-communist Socialists won a landslide in the June and July polls, all but ousting President Sali Berisha's Democrats from parliament. Some Western diplomats have voiced fears Berisha's supporters might opt for a destructive rather than constructive opposition.
